text: What is the World Wide Web (WWW)?
optionA: The same as the internet
optionB: A collection of web pages and resources accessed via the internet using HTTP/HTTPS
optionC: A type of internet connection
optionD: A network cable standard
explanation: The WWW is a service that runs on top of the internet; consisting of web pages linked by hyperlinks and accessed via browsers using HTTP or HTTPS.

text: What does HTTP stand for?
optionA: High Transfer Text Protocol
optionB: HyperText Transfer Protocol
optionC: Hyper Terminal Transfer Process
optionD: HyperText Transmission Protocol
explanation: HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is the protocol used to transfer web pages between a server and a browser.

text: What is the main difference between HTTP and HTTPS?
optionA: HTTPS is faster than HTTP
optionB: HTTPS encrypts data between client and server; HTTP does not
optionC: HTTP is for downloading; HTTPS is for uploading
optionD: HTTPS only works on mobile devices
explanation: HTTPS adds TLS/SSL encryption to HTTP; protecting data from interception during transmission.

text: What is a URL?
optionA: A type of computer virus
optionB: A Uniform Resource Locator — an address that specifies the location of a resource on the internet
optionC: A unique network identifier assigned to a device
optionD: A unit used to measure internet speed
explanation: A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is a web address that includes the protocol; domain name; and optional path to a specific resource.

text: What does a web browser do?
optionA: It stores web pages on a server
optionB: It converts HTML into a human-readable and viewable web page
optionC: It creates web pages for publication
optionD: It filters network traffic for security
explanation: A web browser (e.g. Chrome; Firefox) retrieves HTML files from web servers and renders them as visual pages.

text: What is the role of a web server?
optionA: To request and display web pages
optionB: To store and serve web pages and resources to browsers on request
optionC: To assign IP addresses to devices
optionD: To filter dangerous websites
explanation: A web server hosts web content and responds to HTTP/HTTPS requests from clients (browsers).

text: What is a cookie in the context of web browsing?
optionA: A small program downloaded from a web server
optionB: A type of malware hidden in web pages
optionC: A small text file stored on a user's device by a website to remember information
optionD: A unit of internet bandwidth
explanation: Cookies store information (e.g. login status; preferences) on the user's device; allowing websites to remember state between visits.

text: What is an IP address?
optionA: A web page address (URL)
optionB: A unique numerical label identifying a device on a network
optionC: A type of encryption used for email
optionD: A password required to log in to a network
explanation: An IP address (e.g. 192.168.1.1 for IPv4) uniquely identifies a device on a network and enables packets to be routed correctly.

text: What is a DNS server used for?
optionA: To store emails
optionB: To translate domain names (e.g. www.example.com) into IP addresses
optionC: To encrypt web traffic
optionD: To assign MAC addresses to devices
explanation: DNS (Domain Name System) translates human-readable domain names into numerical IP addresses that routers use.

text: What is the difference between IPv4 and IPv6?
optionA: IPv4 is faster; IPv6 is more secure
optionB: IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses; IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses; allowing far more unique addresses
optionC: IPv4 is used on wireless networks; IPv6 on wired networks
optionD: IPv6 is an older standard replaced by IPv4
explanation: IPv4 supports about 4 billion addresses; IPv6 provides 2^128 addresses — vastly more; developed to cope with the growth of internet-connected devices.

text: What is a static IP address?
optionA: An IP address that changes with every connection
optionB: An IP address that remains the same every time the device connects
optionC: An IP address that is shared by multiple users
optionD: A temporary address used only for local networks
explanation: A static IP is permanently assigned to a device; useful for servers. A dynamic IP is assigned from a pool each session by DHCP.

text: What is cloud computing?
optionA: Running software on a local computer without the internet
optionB: Storing and processing data on remote servers accessed via the internet
optionC: A type of wireless network protocol
optionD: A CPU architecture used in data centres
explanation: Cloud computing provides on-demand access to computing resources (storage; software; processing) over the internet.

text: Which type of cloud is used exclusively by one organisation and not shared with others?
optionA: Public cloud
optionB: Hybrid cloud
optionC: Community cloud
optionD: Private cloud
explanation: A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation; offering more control and security than a public cloud.

text: What is a hybrid cloud?
optionA: A cloud that connects two countries
optionB: A mix of public and private cloud services used together
optionC: A cloud used only for audio and video
optionD: A cloud run entirely on wireless networks
explanation: A hybrid cloud combines public and private cloud services; allowing organisations to use public resources for less-sensitive tasks and private for sensitive data.

text: What is the main purpose of a firewall?
optionA: To speed up internet connections
optionB: To monitor and control incoming and outgoing network traffic based on rules
optionC: To encrypt files stored on a server
optionD: To compress data before transmission
explanation: A firewall enforces rules about which network packets are allowed through; protecting systems from unauthorised access.

text: What is packet switching?
optionA: Sending all data as one large unbroken stream
optionB: Breaking data into packets that can take different routes and are reassembled at the destination
optionC: A type of network cable standard
optionD: A method of encrypting network traffic
explanation: Packet switching splits data into smaller packets; each routed independently through the network and reassembled by the recipient.

text: What information does a data packet header typically contain?
optionA: Only the payload data
optionB: Source address; destination address; packet number and error-checking data
optionC: The user's password and login details
optionD: Only the error-checking checksum
explanation: A packet header carries routing and sequencing information: source IP; destination IP; sequence number; and a checksum for error detection.

text: What is the main advantage of packet switching over circuit switching?
optionA: It always uses the same fixed path
optionB: It can use multiple routes; making better use of network capacity and recovering from failures
optionC: It is faster because no routing decisions are made
optionD: It requires less error checking
explanation: Packet switching dynamically routes packets; meaning if one path is busy or fails; packets can take alternative routes.

text: What does the TCP in TCP/IP stand for?
optionA: Transfer Control Protocol
optionB: Transmission Control Protocol
optionC: Terminal Communication Protocol
optionD: Timed Connection Protocol
explanation: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) manages reliable; ordered; and error-checked delivery of data between applications.

text: What is the purpose of the IP protocol in TCP/IP?
optionA: To encrypt data before transmission
optionB: To address packets and route them across interconnected networks
optionC: To ensure packets arrive in the correct order
optionD: To compress data to reduce bandwidth usage
explanation: IP (Internet Protocol) handles addressing and routing — it determines the path packets take through the network.

text: What does parity checking detect in data transmission?
optionA: Missing packets
optionB: A single-bit error in a transmitted data unit
optionC: The order that packets arrive in
optionD: Whether encryption has been applied
explanation: A parity bit is added to make the total number of 1s even (or odd); if the received count differs; a 1-bit error is detected.

text: What is a checksum used for?
optionA: To speed up packet transmission
optionB: To verify that data has not been corrupted during transmission
optionC: To encrypt data before sending
optionD: To assign priority to different packets
explanation: A checksum is a calculated value sent with data; the receiver recalculates it and compares — a mismatch indicates corruption.

text: What does ARQ (Automatic Repeat reQuest) do when errors are detected?
optionA: It discards the corrupted packet and continues
optionB: It automatically requests retransmission of corrupted data
optionC: It corrects the corrupted bits without retransmission
optionD: It slows down transmission to reduce errors
explanation: ARQ error control sends a negative acknowledgement (NAK) when errors are detected; prompting the sender to retransmit.

text: A sender transmits a packet and waits for a response. The receiver sends an ACK. What does ACK mean?
optionA: The packet contained an error and must be resent
optionB: The packet was received successfully
optionC: The receiver is busy and cannot accept data
optionD: The packet was lost and must be resent
explanation: ACK (acknowledgement) means the packet was received and was correct — the sender can proceed with the next packet.

text: What is a router's main function in a network?
optionA: To broadcast all packets to every device
optionB: To forward packets toward their destination based on routing tables
optionC: To assign MAC addresses to network devices
optionD: To convert between analogue and digital signals
explanation: A router reads the destination IP address of each packet and forwards it toward that destination using its routing table.

text: What is a MAC address?
optionA: A temporary address assigned by DHCP
optionB: A permanent hardware address assigned to a network interface card
optionC: An internet address used in URLs
optionD: A media player format for video files
explanation: A MAC (Media Access Control) address is a unique 48-bit hardware identifier permanently assigned to a network interface.

text: What is the purpose of a switch in a network?
optionA: To connect a network to the internet
optionB: To direct network traffic only to the intended device using MAC addresses
optionC: To assign IP addresses to devices
optionD: To encrypt data before transmission
explanation: A switch forwards data frames only to the specific port associated with the destination MAC address; reducing unnecessary traffic.

text: What does VPN stand for and what does it do?
optionA: Virtual Processing Network — speeds up internet access
optionB: Very Private Network — restricts access to one building
optionC: Virtual Private Network — creates an encrypted tunnel over a public network
optionD: Verified Protocol Network — checks if connections are genuine
explanation: A VPN encrypts network traffic between a client and a server; creating a secure private channel over an otherwise public network.

text: What is TLS used for in network communications?
optionA: To assign IP addresses dynamically
optionB: To encrypt data transmitted over a network; e.g. in HTTPS connections
optionC: To filter emails for spam
optionD: To route packets through the fastest path
explanation: TLS (Transport Layer Security) provides encryption; authentication and data integrity for communications — it is what makes HTTPS secure.

text: What is the purpose of encryption in data transmission?
optionA: To compress data to reduce file size
optionB: To scramble data so only the intended recipient can read it
optionC: To speed up data transmission
optionD: To route data packets more efficiently
explanation: Encryption converts data into an unreadable form using a key; protecting it from eavesdropping during transmission.

text: What is the difference between a LAN and a WAN?
optionA: A LAN is wireless; a WAN is wired
optionB: A LAN covers a small area (e.g. a building); a WAN covers a large geographical area
optionC: A LAN is used by businesses; a WAN is used only in homes
optionD: A WAN is faster than a LAN
explanation: LAN (Local Area Network) covers a limited area; WAN (Wide Area Network) connects LANs across large distances.

text: What is a network topology?
optionA: The speed of a network connection
optionB: The physical or logical arrangement of devices in a network
optionC: The type of cable used in a network
optionD: The number of users on a network
explanation: Network topology describes how devices are connected — examples include bus; star; ring and mesh topologies.

text: In a star topology; what happens if the central hub or switch fails?
optionA: Only the two nearest devices lose connection
optionB: The whole network is unable to communicate
optionC: Each device connects directly to its neighbours instead
optionD: Data is rerouted automatically through other nodes
explanation: In a star topology; all devices connect through a central switch. If that switch fails; all network communication stops.

text: What is one advantage of a star topology compared to a bus topology?
optionA: Less cable is needed
optionB: A failure in one node does not affect other nodes
optionC: It is slower but more reliable
optionD: Data cannot be intercepted on a star network
explanation: In a star network; a fault in one node's cable affects only that node; not the rest of the network. On a bus; a cable break stops all communication.

text: What is the purpose of a protocol in networking?
optionA: To physically connect devices
optionB: To set agreed rules that allow devices to communicate with each other
optionC: To increase network speed
optionD: To assign unique MAC addresses
explanation: A protocol is a set of rules governing how data is formatted; transmitted; received and acknowledged between devices.

text: What does DHCP do?
optionA: Encrypts data before transmission
optionB: Automatically assigns IP addresses to devices on a network
optionC: Converts domain names to IP addresses
optionD: Filters network packets for security
explanation: DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) automatically assigns IP addresses; subnet masks and gateway addresses to devices when they join a network.

text: What is the main advantage of a client-server network over a peer-to-peer network?
optionA: Files are shared equally between all computers
optionB: Central management of users; security and data backups is easier
optionC: It requires less expensive hardware
optionD: Every device can connect to the internet independently
explanation: A client-server model provides centralised administration of accounts; permissions; updates and backups; which is more scalable and secure.

text: What is meant by bandwidth in networking?
optionA: The length of network cables
optionB: The maximum amount of data that can be transmitted per unit of time
optionC: The delay before data transfer begins
optionD: The number of devices on a network
explanation: Bandwidth is typically measured in Mbps or Gbps and indicates the capacity of a network connection.

text: What is latency in network communications?
optionA: The maximum bandwidth of a connection
optionB: The time delay between sending and receiving a data packet
optionC: The amount of data lost during transmission
optionD: The speed at which a router processes packets
explanation: Latency (ping) is the round-trip time for a packet; measured in milliseconds. High latency causes delays in real-time applications.

text: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of using a network?
optionA: Users can share peripherals like printers
optionB: Users can access shared files from any device
optionC: Network cables are never needed with Wi-Fi
optionD: Software can be centrally installed and updated
explanation: A network might use wired or wireless connections; the statement that network cables are never needed is false (many networks use both).

text: What output does an AND gate produce when both inputs are 1?
optionC: It depends on a third input
optionD: Undefined
explanation: An AND gate outputs 1 only when ALL inputs are 1. With both inputs at 1; output = 1.

text: What output does an OR gate produce when inputs are 0 and 1?
optionC: It oscillates between 0 and 1
optionD: Undefined
explanation: An OR gate outputs 1 when ANY input is 1. With inputs 0 and 1; output = 1.

text: What is the output of a NOT gate when the input is 0?
optionC: The same as the input
optionD: It has no output
explanation: A NOT gate inverts its input. NOT 0 = 1.

text: Complete the truth table row for NAND with inputs A=1 and B=1. What is the output?
optionD: It is the same as AND
explanation: NAND = NOT AND. AND(1;1)=1; NOT 1 = 0.

text: Complete the truth table row for NOR with inputs A=0 and B=0. What is the output?
optionC: 0 and 1 simultaneously
optionD: Undefined
explanation: NOR = NOT OR. OR(0;0)=0; NOT 0 = 1.

text: A XOR gate has inputs A=1 and B=1. What is the output?
optionC: It is the same as OR
optionD: It is the same as AND
explanation: XOR (exclusive OR) outputs 1 only when inputs are DIFFERENT. With both inputs 1; output = 0.

text: What is the Boolean expression for an AND gate with inputs A and B?
optionA: A + B
optionB: A · B
optionC: A ⊕ B
optionD: Ā
explanation: The AND operation uses multiplication notation A · B (or AB). The output is 1 only when both A AND B are 1.

text: What is the Boolean expression for the output of an OR gate with inputs A and B?
optionA: A + B
optionB: A · B
optionC: A ⊕ B
optionD: A'
explanation: The OR operation uses addition notation A + B. The output is 1 when A OR B (or both) is 1.

text: A logic circuit has three inputs connected to an AND gate; followed by a NOT gate. If all three inputs are 1; what is the final output?
optionD: It is the same as the AND output

text: What does a logic gate truth table show?
optionA: The voltage levels inside a circuit
optionB: All possible input combinations and the corresponding outputs
optionC: The physical layout of a circuit board
optionD: The speed at which a circuit operates
explanation: A truth table systematically lists every combination of inputs and the resulting output for a logic gate or circuit.

text: How many rows does a truth table with 3 inputs require (excluding the header)?
explanation: A truth table needs 2^n rows where n is the number of inputs. 2^3 = 8.

text: A NAND gate is known as a universal gate. What does this mean?
optionA: It can be used in every country without modifications
optionB: Any other logic gate can be built from NAND gates alone
optionC: It has more inputs than any other gate
optionD: It operates at universal voltage levels
explanation: NAND (and NOR) gates are universal because any Boolean function can be implemented using only NAND gates.

text: In Boolean algebra; which of the following represents the NOT A operation?
optionA: A + B
optionB: A · B
optionC: A'
optionD: A ⊕ B
explanation: A' (or Ā) denotes the complement (NOT) of A.

text: What is the output of an XOR gate when inputs are A=0 and B=1?
optionC: It is the same as OR
optionD: It is the same as NAND
explanation: XOR outputs 1 when inputs are DIFFERENT. 0 ≠ 1; so output = 1.

text: What is a half adder used for in digital circuits?
optionA: To subtract two binary numbers
optionB: To add two 1-bit binary inputs and produce a sum bit and a carry bit
optionC: To multiply two binary numbers
optionD: To convert binary to decimal
explanation: A half adder adds two 1-bit inputs; producing a sum (XOR of inputs) and a carry (AND of inputs).

text: What is an algorithm?
optionA: A programming language used to write software
optionB: A step-by-step set of instructions for solving a problem
optionC: A type of computer hardware component
optionD: A database management system
explanation: An algorithm is a finite; ordered set of unambiguous instructions that solves a problem or achieves a task.

text: What is the purpose of a flowchart?
optionA: To draw electrical circuit diagrams
optionB: To visually represent the steps and decision points of an algorithm
optionC: To show the physical layout of a network
optionD: To design the user interface of an application
explanation: A flowchart uses standard symbols (ovals; rectangles; diamonds; parallelograms) to visually represent an algorithm's logic and flow.

text: In a flowchart; what shape is typically used to represent a decision?
optionA: Rectangle
optionB: Oval
optionC: Diamond
optionD: Parallelogram
explanation: Diamond shapes in flowcharts represent decisions (YES/NO branches); such as IF conditions.

text: What does a trace table help with?
optionA: Drawing the layout of a program's user interface
optionB: Tracking variable values step by step as an algorithm runs
optionC: Testing whether a network is correctly configured
optionD: Measuring the execution speed of a program
explanation: A trace table records variable values after each step of an algorithm; helping identify logic errors by hand.

text: What is a linear (sequential) search?
optionA: Searching through sorted data using a divide-and-conquer approach
optionB: Checking each item in a list one by one until the target is found or the list ends
optionC: Sorting a list before searching it
optionD: Using an index to jump directly to an item
explanation: Linear search starts at the first element and checks each one in order. It works on unsorted lists but is slow for large datasets.

text: How does a binary search work?
optionA: It checks every element from the first to the last
optionB: It divides the sorted list in half; discards the half that cannot contain the target; and repeats
optionC: It sorts the list first then returns the first element
optionD: It uses a hash function to find the target
explanation: Binary search repeatedly halves a sorted list; comparing the target with the midpoint value and discarding the half where the target cannot be.

text: What precondition is REQUIRED for a binary search to work?
optionA: The list must contain only numbers
optionB: The list must be sorted in order
optionC: The list must have fewer than 100 items
optionD: The list must be stored in a 2D array
explanation: Binary search requires the list to be sorted; otherwise the halving logic cannot correctly discard irrelevant sections.

text: What is the worst-case number of comparisons for a linear search on a list of 1000 items?
explanation: In the worst case; the target is the last item or not present; requiring 1000 comparisons.

text: How does a bubble sort work?
optionA: It repeatedly finds the minimum value and moves it to the front
optionB: It repeatedly compares adjacent pairs of elements and swaps them if they are in the wrong order
optionC: It splits the list into halves and merges them in order
optionD: It inserts each element into its correct position one at a time
explanation: Bubble sort passes through the list multiple times; swapping adjacent elements if they are out of order; until no swaps are needed.

text: What is the purpose of a merge sort?
optionA: To find a value in an unsorted list
optionB: To divide a list into halves; sort each recursively; then merge them back in order
optionC: To remove duplicates from a list
optionD: To rearrange items randomly
explanation: Merge sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm: it splits the list; recursively sorts each half; then merges the two sorted halves.

text: Which sorting algorithm is generally more efficient for large lists: bubble sort or merge sort?
optionA: Bubble sort; because it uses less memory
optionB: Merge sort; because it has better time complexity for large datasets
optionC: They are equally efficient for all sizes
optionD: Bubble sort; because each pass is simpler
explanation: Merge sort has O(n log n) time complexity; bubble sort is O(n²) in the worst case — merge sort is much faster on large datasets.

text: What is an insertion sort?
optionA: A sort that inserts the list into a database
optionB: A sort that builds a sorted list by picking each unsorted element and inserting it into its correct position
optionC: A sort that only works on linked lists
optionD: A sort that removes and reinserts duplicate values
explanation: Insertion sort builds the sorted output one item at a time; picking each new element and inserting it in the correct place in the already-sorted portion.

text: In programming; what is a variable?
optionA: A fixed value that never changes
optionB: A named storage location in memory that holds a value which can change
optionC: A keyword used to define a function
optionD: A step in an algorithm
explanation: A variable is a named memory location that stores a value; the value can be read and updated during program execution.

text: What is the difference between an integer and a float (real) data type?
optionA: An integer can store letters; a float cannot
optionB: An integer stores whole numbers; a float stores numbers with a decimal component
optionC: A float uses less memory than an integer
optionD: An integer can be negative; a float cannot
explanation: Integer types hold whole numbers (e.g. 5; −3); float/real types hold numbers with fractional parts (e.g. 3.14).

text: What is a Boolean data type?
optionA: A type that stores very large numbers
optionB: A type that stores only two values: TRUE or FALSE
optionC: A type that stores a single character
optionD: A type that stores sequences of characters
explanation: Boolean represents a logical state: TRUE or FALSE (also represented as 1 or 0).

text: What is a string data type?
optionA: A sequence of characters
optionB: A whole number
optionC: A logical true/false value
optionD: A floating-point number
explanation: A string is an ordered sequence of characters (letters; digits; symbols) enclosed in quotes in most languages.

text: What is an IF statement used for in programming?
optionA: To repeat a block of code a fixed number of times
optionB: To execute different blocks of code depending on whether a condition is true or false
optionC: To define a new function or procedure
optionD: To input data from the user
explanation: An IF statement is a selection construct that tests a condition and branches execution accordingly.

text: What does a FOR loop do?
optionA: It runs until a condition becomes false
optionB: It repeats a block of code a fixed number of times
optionC: It calls a function repeatedly
optionD: It waits for user input
explanation: A FOR loop (count-controlled loop) iterates a specified number of times; often using a counter variable.

text: What does a WHILE loop do?
optionA: It runs exactly once
optionB: It repeats a block of code as long as a condition remains true
optionC: It repeats a block of code a fixed number of times
optionD: It only runs when a variable is equal to zero
explanation: A WHILE loop (condition-controlled loop) tests its condition before each iteration and continues as long as it is TRUE.

text: What is a procedure in programming?
optionA: A variable that stores multiple values
optionB: A self-contained block of code that performs a task and can be called by name
optionC: A type of loop that runs backwards
optionD: A data structure for sorting lists
explanation: A procedure (or subroutine) groups reusable code under a name; reducing duplication and improving program structure.

text: What is the difference between a procedure and a function?
optionA: There is no difference — the terms are interchangeable
optionB: A function returns a value; a procedure does not (or returns nothing)
optionC: A procedure returns a value; a function does not
optionD: A function is written in Python; a procedure is written in pseudocode
explanation: A function performs a task AND returns a value to the caller; a procedure performs a task but does not return a value.

text: What is an array?
optionA: A single value stored under one name
optionB: An ordered collection of values of the same type stored under one name and accessed by index
optionC: A type of loop in programming
optionD: A keyword used to declare variables
explanation: An array stores multiple values of the same data type; each accessed by its index (position number).

text: What is the difference between a local and a global variable?
optionA: A local variable is faster than a global variable
optionB: A local variable is only accessible within the subprogram where it is declared; a global is accessible throughout the whole program
optionC: A global variable can only store integers
optionD: A local variable never changes its value
explanation: Local variables exist only within their defining subprogram and are destroyed when it ends. Global variables persist throughout the program.

text: What is a syntax error in a program?
optionA: An error caused by incorrect logic that produces the wrong result
optionB: An error that occurs because the program runs out of memory
optionC: An error caused by code that violates the grammar rules of the programming language
optionD: An error that occurs only when the user enters invalid input
explanation: Syntax errors (e.g. missing colon; wrong indentation in Python) prevent the program from being parsed or compiled.

text: What is a logic error in a program?
optionA: An error that stops the program from running
optionB: An error where the program runs successfully but produces incorrect results
optionC: An error caused by missing punctuation
optionD: An error that occurs when memory is full
explanation: A logic error means the code runs without crashing but the algorithm is wrong — e.g. using + instead of − in a calculation.

text: What is a runtime error?
optionA: An error detected when the program is compiled
optionB: An error that occurs while the program is executing; causing it to crash
optionC: An error in the algorithm that produces wrong output
optionD: An error caused by incorrect variable names
explanation: Runtime errors occur during execution — examples include division by zero; accessing an index out of range; or running out of memory.

text: What does the CIA triad stand for in cybersecurity?
optionA: Computing; Internet; Automation
optionB: Confidentiality; Integrity; Availability
optionC: Cryptography; Intrusion; Authentication
optionD: Control; Inspection; Authorisation
explanation: The CIA triad is the three core principles of information security: Confidentiality (data is private); Integrity (data is unaltered) and Availability (data is accessible when needed).

text: What is a phishing attack?
optionA: Infecting a computer with self-replicating software
optionB: Tricking a user into revealing sensitive information by pretending to be a trustworthy source
optionC: Intercepting and reading data as it is transmitted across a network
optionD: Overloading a server with requests until it crashes
explanation: Phishing uses deceptive emails; messages or websites that impersonate legitimate entities to steal login credentials or personal data.

text: What is a denial of service (DoS) attack?
optionA: Stealing passwords using fake login pages
optionB: Flooding a server with traffic to make it unavailable to legitimate users
optionC: Installing malware on a device without the user's knowledge
optionD: Intercepting messages between two parties
explanation: A DoS attack overwhelms a target system with fake requests; exhausting its resources and preventing normal service.

text: What is SQL injection?
optionA: A method of compressing SQL database files
optionB: An attack that inserts malicious SQL code into a web form input to manipulate a database
optionC: A type of encryption used to secure databases
optionD: A tool for migrating data between databases
explanation: SQL injection exploits web forms that pass user input directly to SQL queries; allowing attackers to access; modify or delete database contents.

text: What is two-factor authentication (2FA)?
optionA: Using two separate passwords for one account
optionB: Requiring two forms of verification (e.g. password + code sent to phone) to log in
optionC: Using one password on two different devices
optionD: A password manager that stores two accounts
explanation: 2FA adds a second verification step beyond a password; typically something you know (password) plus something you have (phone code) or are (biometric).

text: What is the purpose of data encryption in cybersecurity?
optionA: To compress files to save storage space
optionB: To scramble data so that only authorised parties with the correct key can read it
optionC: To speed up data transmission
optionD: To back up data to multiple locations
explanation: Encryption transforms plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key; ensuring that intercepted data cannot be read without decryption.

text: What is a brute force attack?
optionA: An attack that uses physical force to access a building
optionB: A method of systematically trying every possible password combination until the correct one is found
optionC: An attack that exploits vulnerabilities in network protocols
optionD: A type of social engineering attack
explanation: Brute force attacks try every possible combination of characters until a password is guessed; they are defeated by strong (long; complex) passwords and account lockout policies.

text: What is malware?
optionA: Any software that is out of date
optionB: Software specifically designed to disrupt; damage or gain unauthorised access to a system
optionC: A type of encryption algorithm
optionD: Software that improves computer performance
explanation: Malware (malicious software) includes viruses; worms; ransomware; spyware and trojans — all designed to harm or exploit systems.
